newsitem.title: ITALY: Alitalia vows fair play after fine.
newsitem.headline: Alitalia vows fair play after fine.

text.p: Italian flag carrier Alitalia said on Thursday it was committed to fair play after the national anti-trust authority fined the group 415 million lire ($277,000) for breaching competition rules.
Alitalia managing director Domenico Cempella declined to comment on the details of the ruling, which referred to a period before he took charge of the loss-making airline in February.
But he said Alitalia, which is implementing a radical restructuring plan, did not want "any kind of privilege".
"My Alitalia wants to carve its position in the market based only on its own professionalism and competitiveness," he said.
Alitalia had already handed back to the government responsibility for managing take-off and landing slots to avoid foul play, Cempella added.
In a damning report released earlier, the anti-trust body said Alitalia had "impeded, blocked and restricted" the arrival of new national airlines into the market.

It launched an investigation in February after small Italian private airlines Air One and Meridiana complained that Alitalia was hindering their operations. The body, headed by former prime minister Giuliano Amato, found in their favour, saying Alitalia had sought to block competition in three ways.
It said Alitalia, which was given the task of allocating slots at Italian airports in 1971, had used this privilege to its advantage -- especially at Milan's main Linate airport.

It found that Alitalia had "systematically" timetabled its own flights to take customers from rivals Meridiana and Aliadriatica, making sure its aircraft left between five to 10 minutes before those of its competitors on a number of routes.

Because of this, Aliadriatica, now renamed Air One, had been forced to abandon its services between Linate and the southern Italian cities of Brindisi and Lamezia, leaving Alitalia the sole carrier on those destinations.
Similar tactics had forced Meridiana to drop its Rome-Venice and Rome-Palermo flights, the anti-trust body said.

Finally, Alitalia had tried to snarl Aliadriatica's take off in southern Italy last year by ordering travel agents in the area not to print Aliadriatica tickets on Alitalia machines -- the only ticketing service available at that time.
The anti-trust body said Alitalia had now dropped the practice and had also offered to give up its slot-allocation role, but it nonetheless slapped a fine on the company.
It was the second time Alitalia had fallen foul of the anti-trust authority. In 1994, the Rome-based watchdog forced the company to change pricing levels on its Milan-Rome route.
Alitalia is speeding towards its ninth successive year of losses and last week unveiled a new, low-cost operating company which will eventually absorb all passenger activities.
